Introduction
According to European Directive 2008/98/EC (European 
Council, 2008), landfilling of municipal solid waste (MSW) is 
the least desirable management technology. In addition, European 
Directive 1999/31/EC (European Council, 1999) requires that 
organics should be diverted from the MSW stream sent to the 
landfills. In some European countries (e.g. Germany, Sweden), 
MSW should not be landfilled unless it is extensively pretreated 
to reduce its organic load below a certain threshold value. For 
example, in Germany and Sweden, the total organic carbon of 
MSW prior to landfilling should be less than 18% and 10% (dry 
weight basis) respectively (Fricke et  al., 2005; Praagh et  al., 
2009). As a result, mechanical–biological pretreatment, and par­
ticularly the aerobic biological treatment (ABT), has gained a lot 
of attention as a pretreatment technique prior to landfilling. The 
goal of long-term ABT is to produce a stabilized or semi-stabi­
lized product that can be safely disposed of to a zero emission 
(i.e. final storage or sustainable) landfill (De Gioannis et  al., 
2009; Scaglia et al., 2010; Schievano et al., 2008; Zach et al., 
2000). It is well established that anaerobic emissions of MSW 
that has been aerobically pretreated differ from those of untreated 
waste (Brinkmann et al., 1995; Carlsson et al., 2012; Corti et al., 
2009; De Gioannis et  al., 2009; Güelfo et  al., 2011; Komilis 
et  al., 1999; Leikam and Stegmann, 1995; Rieger and 
Bidlingmaier, 1995; Scaglia et  al., 2010; Scharff et  al., 1995; 
Zach et al., 2000). Binner and Zach (1999) performed experi­
ments with laboratory-scale reactors and showed that the 90-day 
biogas yield of raw MSW decreased from 129 NL dry kg-1 to 10 
NL dry kg-1 after 9 weeks of aerobic biological treatment. Zach 
et al. (2000) also showed that the 240-day biogas yield decreased 
by an order of magnitude after 20 weeks of ABT. However, Adani 
et al. (2004) showed that the 90-day biogas yield (measured in 
60-mL vials) of untreated MSW and of MSW treated aerobically 
for 10 days and 21 days increased from 6 L dry kg-1 to 6.8 and 20 
L dry kg-1 respectively. This finding agrees with previous work 
by Adani et al. (2000), and can likely be explained by the fact that 
Aerobic biological pretreatment of 
municipal solid waste with a high content of 
putrescibles: effect on landfill emissions
Spyridoula Gerassimidou, Alexandros Evangelou and 
Dimitrios Komilis
Abstract
The objective of this work was to study the effect of aerobic biological pretreatment on the emissions of municipal solid waste (MSW) 
with a high content of putrescibles after landfilling. For this purpose, the organic fraction of MSW was simulated by a mixture of food 
waste and office paper at a 2.4:1 wet weight ratio. MSW was first pretreated aerobically for three different time periods (8, 45 and 
90 days) resulting in organic matter reductions equal to 15%, 45% and 81% respectively. MSW were then placed in 160-L air-tight 
anaerobic bioreactors. The control anaerobic bioreactors contained untreated MSW. Anaerobic experiments lasted from 300 to 550 
days. Results showed that the biogas production from untreated MSW was 372 NL dry kg-1 (average of two replications) after 530 
days. The MSW that was pretreated aerobically for 45 days and 90 days yielded 130 and 62 NL dry kg-1 of biogas after 310 days and 
230 days respectively. However, the 8-day (very short-term) pretreatment period led to an increase of the biogas yield (550 NL dry kg-
1 after 340 days) compared with that of raw refuse. All three runs with aerobically pretreated MSW reached the steady methanogenic 
phase faster than raw MSW. Leachate emissions were significantly lower in the aerobically-pretreated MSWthan the untreated ones. 
The leachate ammonium concentrations had an increasing trend in all anaerobic reactors and reached a plateau of between 2 and 3.5 
g L-1 at the end of the process.
Keywords
Biogas yields, bioreactor landfill, sustainable landfilling, zero emission landfills

the duration of the anaerobic experiment should have been longer 
than 90 days to allow the establishment of methanogenesis in the 
raw refuse samples. Short-term (2-week) aerobic pretreatment 
has been also found to decrease the methane (CH4) generation lag 
time and to accelerate the start up of a dry anaerobic system with 
the organic fraction of MSW (Brummeler and Koster, 1990); 
however, the short pretreatment led to a significant loss (40%) of 
the potential CH4 yield of the untreated waste.
Despite the amount of research, the effect of aerobic pretreat­
ment on landfill emissions of MSW that contains a high percent­
age of putrescibles, such as Hellenic MSW (HMD, 2003), has not 
been investigated. In addition, it appears that there is limited 
information on the effect of very short-term (e.g. 1 week) aerobic 
pretreatment periods on the subsequent anaerobic emissions. The 
objective of this work was, therefore, to quantify gaseous and 
leachable landfill emissions of aerobically pretreated MSW that 
contained a high percentage of putrescibles after 8, 45 and 90 
days of ABT periods. A relationship between the organic matter 
(OM) reduction achieved during the ABT phases and the subse­
quent anaerobic emissions can aid decision makers in determin­
ing the fate of the pretreated MSW (i.e. either to obtain a product 
with enhanced biogas potential for disposal to a bioreactor land­
fill or a product with reduced anaerobic emissions for disposal to 
a zero emission landfill).
Materials and methods
Simulation of the organic fraction of MSW
The organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) was 
simulated using a mixture of wasted office paper (OFP) and food 
waste (FW). OFP was collected from faculty offices and was man­
ually cut to pieces less than 2.5 cm in size. Fifty kilograms of 
composite FW batches was collected from the university restau­
rant over a 1-week period. Each batch of FW and OFP was char­
acterized separately prior to the initiation of a run. The simulated 
OFMSW contained FW and OFP at a 2.4:1 ratio, on a wet weight 
basis, which is the approximate ratio of these components in the 
Hellenic MSW (HMD, 2003). We simulated the organic fraction 
of MSW in order to maintain a consistent and well controlled ini­
tial composition of refuse throughout the experiments and to 
decrease the need of many replicates in our runs. Inorganics were 
not included in our simulated composition, as they do not contrib­
ute to the anaerobic emissions that we measured in this work.
Aerobic pretreatment
The aerobic reactors used to biologically pretreat (compost) the 
waste were made of high density polyethylene and had a volume 
of 200 L. A screen was placed 10 cm above the bottom of the 
reactor to create an air-plenum. Ambient air at a flow rate of 2 L 
min-1 was continuously pumped via a compressor to the bottom 
of the reactor. Each aerobic digester contained 20 (wet) kg of 
simulated OFMSW. Thickened aerobic sludge (obtained from a 
nearby wastewater treatment plant) was added to the mixtures of 
all aerobic runs to inoculate their contents in order to speed up 
the process and to increase initial moisture to 55–60% (wet 
weight basis). The sludge had a moisture content of 98.2% [wet 
weight (ww)] and an OM content of 80.5% [dry weight (dw)]. 
The aerobic reactors were filled to two-thirds of their total vol­
ume and were placed in a temperature controlled room at 35°C 
± 2°C. The aerobic reactor setup is explained in detail in Komilis 
et al. (2011).
Anaerobic bioreactors
The stainless steel anaerobic bioreactors were air tight and had a 
volume of 165 L. The OFMSW was placed on top of a screen that 
was located 6 cm above the bottom of the reactor. The generated 
biogas exited the bioreactors from a top valve and passed through 
a cumulative drum-type low flowrate gas meter by Ritter (model 
TG05/5, Ritter, Bochum, Germany). The gas flowmeters were 
equipped with a thermometer to measure the temperature of the 
exiting gas. Actual biogas volumes were converted to normal 
conditions (0°C, 1 atm) and were reported in NL dry kg-1 of mix­
ture. The composition of the gas was measured via a portable gas 
analyzer (GA94A, Geotechnical Instruments, Leamington, UK)
during the same time that the cumulative gas volume was 
recorded. The gas analyzer was checked periodically using a 
standard gas of methane (CH4):carbon dioxide (CO2) at 
49.9%:50.1% (v/v), respectively, and a mixture of oxygen 
(O2):nitrogen (N2) containing O2 at 8.06% (v/v).
Water was added to the contents of all anaerobic runs to reach 
an initial moisture content of between 70% and 75% (ww) to stim­
ulate anaerobiosis, to decrease experimental times and to aid in 
the production of adequate amounts of leachate (Barlaz et  al., 
1992). Leachate was removed by drainage at the bottom of the 
reactor every 20–25 days. After collecting small leachate amounts 
for analysis, the remaining leachate was manually re-circulated 
back into the reactor from a valve on the top cover. Whenever 
leachate pH was below 5.5, neutralization was performed by add­
ing aliquots of a 1 N sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) liquid solution 
to reach a close to neutral pH (between 6.8 and 7.2). The anaero­
bic reactors were designated as R0, R8, R45 and R90, in which the 
number indicates the duration of the aerobic pretreatment period 
in days. The total wet masses placed in the anaerobic bioreactors 
(including the water added to reach the high initial moisture con­
tent) ranged from 11.8 kg (R90) to 50.2 kg (R0a), which corre­
sponded to dry masses equal to 3.0 and 12.7 kg respectively. The 
amounts of the aerobically pretreated end-products that were 
placed in the subsequent anaerobic reactors varied as a result of 
the different dry weight reductions achieved within each aerobic 
reactor. The bulk density of the material placed in the anaerobic 
reactors ranged from 400 (R0) to 600 kg m-3 (R90) and depended 
on the extent of the aerobic decomposition. The anaerobic experi­
ments were terminated when the biogas production rates were 
kept below 0.2 NL dry kg-1d-1 for five successive days. All anaero­
bic experiments were performed in a temperature controlled room 
at the mesophilic temperature range (35°C ± 2°C). The anaerobic 
reactors were run on a batch mode and simulated a MSW landfill 
at optimal moisture contents. The reproducibility of the anaerobic

system setup was tested by running two replicate anaerobic reac­
tors (R0a, R0b) at different time periods under the same condi­
tions, and with precisely the same source materials and amounts.
Analytical methods
Solids sampling was performed using a sequential quartering 
procedure. The moisture content was measured at 75°C until con­
stant weight. The dried solids were then ground using a solids’ 
cutting mill (RETSCH, Haan,Germany) with a 1.5-mm mesh size 
screen and the OM content was measured via the loss on ignition 
at 550°C for 2 h. Elemental analysis was performed using an 
elemental analyzer (Thermo Electron, Waltham, MA, USA, 
model: EA-1110 CHNS-O) according to Komilis et al. (2012). 
Leachate pH was measured with a portable pH-meter (WTW, 
Weilheim, Germany). The total 5-day biochemical oxygen 
demand (BOD5), total chemical oxygen demand (COD) and 
ammonium (N-NH4+) concentrations of the leachates were meas­
ured using standard methods (APHA and AWWA, 1998). The dry 
matter and OM reduction achieved during the aerobic and anaer­
obic experiments were calculated based on the principle of ash 
conservation.
Results and discussion
Degradation of solid waste in the aerobic 
pretreatment reactors
The properties of the source materials used to simulate the 
MSW are shown in Table 1. At the end of the aerobic experi­
ments (i.e. after 8, 45 and 90 days), the final moisture contents 
of the remaining substrates ranged from 45% to 66% (ww). 
The properties of the end materials and the dry matter 
reduction calculated during the aerobic experiments are 
included in Table 2. According to Table 2, the higher the extent 
of aerobic pretreatment, the higher were the losses of dry 
mass, OM, carbon and nitrogen within the aerobic reactors. 
The final OM content of the aerobically pretreated mixtures 
ranged from 84% dw to 54% dw for the 8- and 90-day aerobic 
pretreatment period runs. As expected, the 90-day aerobic pre­
treatment period led to the highest dry matter and OM reduc­
tion (69% and 81% respectively) (see Table 2). The total 
nitrogen reduction achieved during the aerobic phases ranged 
from 10.5% (8-day pretreatment) to 59% (90-day aerobic pre­
treatment). Gas content measurements that were performed in 
the headspace of all aerobic reactors showed that the CO2 con­
tent peaked at 5–6% v/v after 4–5 days and O2 content reached 
a minimum of 11–13% v/v at the same time. No CH4 was 
detected throughout the aerobic pretreatment process. The 
good replication of the aerobic reactor setup had been con­
firmed in a previous study (Komilis et al., 2011).
Biogas yields and composition 
Table 3 includes the biogas yields measured at the end of the five 
anaerobic runs.
Figures 1 and 2 illustrate the normalized CH4 and CO2 cumu­
lative yields of all five anaerobic experiments versus time. 
According to Figure 1 and Table 3, reproducibility of the anaero­
bic system was relatively weak, as the biogas yields from repli­
cate runs R0a and R0b differed by 40% after 530 days. A difficulty 
in replicating pilot-scale anaerobic reactors was also noted by 
Barlaz et al. (1987) during landfill simulation experiments with 
208-L drums. Figure 1 reveals that the onset of the steady metha­
nogenesis occurred at 160 days for R0a, whilst it occurred at 280

of experimental time, R8 produced greater amounts of biogas 
compared with both R0 runs over the same time period. This is 
likely attributed to the fact that the 8-day aerobic pretreatment 
period removed most of the readily degradable carbon (RDC), 
which is responsible for the fast acid production and the rapid pH 
decrease that inhibits methanogenesis (Brummeler and Koster, 
1990; Komilis et  al., 1999). The 45-day aerobic pretreatment 
period (see Figure 2) led to an even quicker establishment of the 
steady methanogenic phase, as the CH4 content reached values 
greater than 40% after only 38 days. However, an intermediate 
opening of R45 for inspection purposes on day 80 temporarily 
disrupted methanogenesis and led to sharp decreases of the CH4 
and CO2 contents. Still, CH4 generation rapidly recovered and 
reached contents above 30% after day 150. A gradual decrease in 
the contents of both CH4 and CO2 was measured in R45 after the 
260th day until the termination of the run.
R90 yielded even smaller amounts of biogas, which reached 
62 NL dry kg-1 after 230 days. In R90, CH4 rapidly peaked after 
43 days, but never exceeded 35% v/v; it then gradually decreased 
to values close to 0% until the termination of the experiment. An 
almost similar profile was also observed for the CO2. Most of the 
biogas of R90 was generated during the first 100 days and biogas 
generation rates decreased significantly after 150 days. The final 
OM content of the anaerobic residue in R90 was 37% (dw), 
whilst the dry mass and OM reductions that occurred within that 
reactor were 25% and 46% respectively (see Table 3). Therefore, 
it appears that the 45- and 90-day aerobic pretreatment periods 
led to a 65% and 84% biogas yield reduction compared with the 
average biogas yield of raw refuse. More specifically, CH4 yield 
decreased by 70% and 85% in the R45 and R90 runs, respec­
tively, compared with the average CH4 yield of R0 (194 NL dry 
kg-1). CO2 yields decreased by 60% and 80% in R45 and R90, 
respectively, compared with that of R0 (178 NL dry kg-1). In 
addition, the methanogenesis lag times in R45 and R90 were 
highly shortened (lasted 40 days) compared with that of R0 (160 
days). O2 contents decreased to 0% only a few hours after the 
initiation of all anaerobic reactors and remained at that level 
throughout the experiments.
Similar effects of long-term aerobic pretreatment have been 
found by Binner and Zach (1999), Zach et al. (2000), Jokela et al. 
(2002) and Corti et al. (2009). For example, Jokela et al. (2002) 
observed that the CH4 potential decreased 10 times when an aero­
bic pretreatment step was first applied (i.e. a decrease from 410 L 
CH4 dry kg-1 to 41 L CH4 dry kg-1). However, the results of Jokela 
et  al. (2002) were based on biochemical CH4 potential tests, 
which are known to result in higher biogas yields than pilot-scale 
anaerobic reactors. Other short-term (2-week) aerobic pretreat­
ment studies have also observed a fast establishment of methano­
genesis and a reduction of the biogas yield compared with that of 
raw MSW (Brummeler and Koster, 1990). However, our results 
show that a very short-term (8-day) aerobic pretreatment of 
MSW with a high content of putrescibles (which corresponds to 
a 15% OM reduction) can result not only in the fast establishment 
of methanogenesis but also in an increase of the biogas yield 
compared with that of raw MSW over a period of 1.5 years. 
These findings agree with Adani et al. (2004), who had, however, 
performed their anaerobic experiments in small vials and used 
only a 90-day experimental period.
Leachate properties
Figure 3 presents the BOD5 concentration, the BOD5/COD ratio, 
the pH and the N-NH4+ concentrations of the leachates versus 
time for all anaerobic reactors. The average leachate volume col­
lected per reactor at each recirculation event was 0.70 (R0a), 1.3 
(R0b), 0.71 (R8), 1.5 (R45) and 0.52 L dry kg-1 (R90). According 
to Figure 3a, the highest BOD5 concentrations were recorded for 
the replicate R0a and R0b runs that contained the untreated 
waste. This is expected, as the RDC of the putrescibles contained 
in the raw refuse is converted to acids during hydrolysis and aci­
dogenesis. The BOD5 concentration profiles of the two replicate 
R0 runs were similar. That is, BOD5 peaked at 50–100 days as 
organic acids started to be generated, lowering pH (see Figure 
3C). BOD5 concentrations greater than 20 g L-1 were measured 
during the first 150 days in both R0 runs. BOD5 then gradually 
decreased until the 300th day. A slow increasing trend was 
observed later on in R0 until the termination of the experiment, 
which could be attributed to the initiation of the breakdown of the 
moderately degradable organic carbon, which hydrolyses at 
slower rates than the RDC. However, the BOD5 contents of all 
other reactors (R8, R45, R90) remained less than 5 g L-1 through­
out the experiment. The BOD5 concentration of the R45, in par­
ticular, reached its maximum value on the 10th day (5.1 g L-1) 
and gradually decreased later on. Similarly, the R90 run observed 
its maximum BOD5 content (4.5 g L-1) on the 26th day. According 
to Figure 3B, there were large fluctuations in the BOD5/COD 
ratios for all runs and, particularly, for the R0 runs. For runs R8, 
R45 and R90, a decreasing trend of the BOD5/COD ratio is evi­
dent, with maximum values at 0.8 (for R90 only) at the beginning 
of the process and a gradual decrease to less than 0.3 later on. The 
BOD5/COD ratio decreasing trends to final values close to 0.1 are 
typical for aging landfills (McBean et  al., 1995, p. 307). The 
BOD5/COD ratio of the R0b decreased to values less than 0.2 
during the middle of the run, but increased to values greater than 
0.7 at the final stages, probably owing to the decomposition of 
moderately degradable carbon.
The characteristic pH decrease (see Figure 3C) that occurs 
during anaerobic acidogenesis was recorded during the first 100 
days for all runs, except R90. Actually, leachate pH ranged from 
4.0 to 5.5 in the R0 runs during the first 80 days, despite the con­
tinuous neutralization with Na2CO3 over that time. The leachate 
from the R0a run reached a close-to-neutral pH after 180 days, 
which was the approximate time of the initiation of the steady 
methanogenic phase. Similarly, leachate from the R0b reactor 
reached a neutral pH after 280 days, which was, again, the 
approximate time of initiation of the steady methanogenic phase 
for that run. The above agree well with the established landfill 
degradation theory, which states that methanogenesis in landfills

Gerassimidou et al.	
789
starts right after acidogenesis, as acidic pH increases to neutral 
levels owing to the gradual consumption of acids by methano­
gens (Farquhar and Rovers, 1997). During the steady methano­
genic phase, pH values remained above 7, with a slight increasing 
trend, for both R0 runs. However, pH started at 5.8 for the R8 and 
R45 runs, and very rapidly increased and remained above 7 for 
the rest of the experiment. The leachate pH of R90 was constantly 
above 7.2, from the start of the experiment, with an increasing 
trend to up to 8.5 at the end of the run. It therefore appears that a 
large amount of RDC was removed during the aerobic pretreat­
ment stage, which prevented excessive acid formation during the 
subsequent anaerobic stage.
The N-NH4+ concentrations for all runs observed an increas­
ing trend with time until a plateau was always reached. This 
ammonium accumulation has also been observed by other 
researchers (Mahar et al., 2009), and is explained by the low bio­
mass yield during anaerobiosis and the lack of nitrification. 
Although some ammonia (NH3) gaseous emissions may occur 
(though NH3 was not measured in this work), the lack of the 
above processes inevitably led to NH4+ accumulation. As indi­
cated in Figure 3D, the NH4+ concentration in both R0 runs 
observed an increasing trend from 0.05 g L-1 up to 4.5 g L-1 (for 
R0b). R0b resulted in leachate that had almost twice as high as 
NH4+ concentration compared with the R0a, although the trends 
were similar for both runs. The NH4+ of the leachates from the R8 
and R45 runs also observed an increasing trend to concentrations 
of up to 2.5 g L-1 (R8). Strangely, the NH4+ content in R90 almost 
doubled during the last two sampling events to values up to 3.5 g 
L-1. This is probably attributed to the low amounts of leachate 
generated at the end of the R90 run, which led to an inevitable 
concentration of the NH4+ ions. The NH4+ concentration in the 
leachate of R45 reached a plateau at 1.5 g L-1 after 100 days.
Some similarities of the 8-day pretreatment stage with the 
two-stage anaerobic digestion process do exist. In the two-step 
anaerobic digestion, hydrolysis is performed in a separate reactor 
and the hydrolyzed material is then supplied under control to the 
methanogenic reactor so as not to inhibit methanogenesis from a 
rapid pH decrease (Merlino et al., 2013). In our case, the 8-day 
aerobic pretreatment reactor hydrolyzed some of the readily 
degradable organics to sugars and acids, which were eventually 
decomposed to CO2. Thus, less readily degradable carbon was 
loaded to the subsequent anaerobic reactors and methanogenesis 
inhibition was prevented.
Decrease of solids during the aerobic and 
anaerobic processes
Figure 4A shows that the highest OM content decrease occurred 
during the 90-day aerobic pretreatment step (i.e. OM decreased 
from 86% dw to 53% dw), which corresponds to an 80% decrease 
(see Table 2). The OM content of the anaerobic end product of 
R90 was close to 38% dw, the lowest value among all OM con­
tents of the anaerobic residues, then followed the end product of 
R8 with an OM content of 42.1% (dw). Figure 4B shows the 
relationship between the biogas yields of all five anaerobic reac­
tors with the OM decrease achieved during the ABT phase.

According to Figure 4B, the short-term (8-day) aerobic pretreat­
ment step (15% OM decrease) led to an enhancement of biogas 
generation compared with raw refuse, which partly agrees with 
Adani et al. (2004), who had also used short-term aerobic pre­
treatment periods. However, higher OM reduction (above 40%) 
led to decreased biogas yields, as has been clearly shown by sev­
eral researchers (Binner and Zach, 1999; Carlsson et al., 2012; 
De Gioannis et al., 2009; Mahar et al., 2009; Zach et al., 2000). 
Therefore, an at least 40% OM decrease has to be achieved dur­
ing an ABT phase to generate waste for disposition to a zero 
emission landfill. However, if the goal is to enhance biogas gen­
eration, then the OM decrease of MSW with high amounts of 
putrescibles should not exceed 15%. Although some carbon is 
inevitably lost during the ABT phase, the benefits from the 
enhanced biogas yields during the first 1–1.5 years would offset 
the carbon lost.
Conclusions
••
A very short-term (8 day) aerobic pretreatment period (that 
corresponded to a 15% OM loss) accelerated the start-up of 
methanogenesis, resulted in non-acidic leachates and led to 
higher biogas yields compared with that of raw MSW.
••
The 45% and 81% OM reduction (that corresponded to 45- 
and 90-day aerobic pretreatment periods respectively) 
reduced the biogas yield of untreated waste by 65% and 84% 
respectively. In addition, the lag time before the onset of 
methanogenesis was 4–5 times shorter in the pretreated waste 
compared with that of untreated waste.
••
The leachate BOD5 concentrations of the pretreated waste 
were all below 5 g L-1, as opposed to that of untreated waste, 
which reached maximum concentrations up to 55 g L-1. 
Leachate NH4+ concentrations showed an increasing trend for 
all runs until they reached a plateau that ranged from 1.5 g L-1 
to 3.5 g L-1.
••
As the aerobic pretreatment period increased, the pH of the 
landfill leachates became less acidic.
